title: Government drafts law to bring back Gram Sarkar village councils
excerpt: The draft Gram Sarkar Act 2026 would create a 17-member council in each of the country’s 41,112 wards. Experts want a pilot first.
content:
The government plans to revive Gram Sarkar, a village-level council first set up in 1980, under a draft law that would put a 17-member body in every ward of every union in Bangladesh, The Daily Star reported on 8 November.

The Local Government Division has prepared the draft Gram Sarkar Act 2026, and officials said it will go to the cabinet soon.

How it would work

  • Size: one Gram Sarkar in each of the 41,112 wards under 4,568 unions, adding up to nearly seven lakh members.
  • Leadership: each council would be led by the ward’s elected Union Parishad member, with the elected woman UP member as adviser.
  • Members: the other 15 members would be elected by at least 10% of the ward’s voters.
  • Roles: community action against crime, violence against women and terrorism, arbitration of local disputes, planning village roads and culverts, and reviewing rural development projects. Each council would report to its Union Parishad.
  • Pay: the draft sets no honorarium. An official said the finance ministry’s view has been sought.

A contested history

Gram Sarkar was introduced under President Ziaur Rahman in 1980 and scrapped a few years later under HM Ershad. A 2003 version, with fully nominated members, was challenged in the High Court, declared unconstitutional and repealed. The new draft draws on both earlier laws but adds elections for most members.

Who said what

Mir Shahe Alam, state minister for local government, rural development and cooperatives, said the councils would help deliver services to marginalised people. “The birth and death registration system faces numerous errors and complications,” he said.

Experts raised two concerns. The draft disqualifies a person only if they were jailed for at least a year for an offence of moral turpitude, so people with shorter sentences could serve after five years. “Allowing someone convicted of an offence to serve as an arbitrator would call the entire system into question,” said Firoz Mia, a former additional secretary.

Abdul Awal Mazumder, a former secretary and public administration researcher, warned that paid arbitrators and local strongmen could capture the councils, and proposed a pilot in 50 upazilas across the eight divisions before any national rollout. A senior official said the government would like to launch nationwide without a pilot, but no decision has been made.

Why it matters

NGOs work closely with Union Parishads and village courts on dispute resolution, social protection lists, women’s safety and local planning. A new elected tier in every ward could become a key partner, or a new gatekeeper, for community programmes. How members are chosen and held accountable will decide which.

What to watch

Whether the cabinet approves the draft, whether it is published for public comment, and whether the government opts for a pilot.

Sources
